headings.text: Why memorise orders of magnitude rather than precise figures?
Where would you put a cache, and when would you decide not to?

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Interactive latency table — Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know

  • Network-side numbers in context — Networking 101: Primer on Latency and Bandwidth

  • Why these numbers drive design — Primer on Web Performance

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The five anchors, in orders of magnitude? L1 ~1 ns · RAM ~100 ns · SSD ~100 µs · Same-DC RTT ~500 µs · Cross-continent ~150 ms.
RAM to same-DC network — how many orders? Roughly 3–4. A network hop costs ~5,000× a memory read.
What decision does this table make for you? Whether to cache, where to cache, and whether a call can be in a hot loop at all.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

The useful version of this isn't a table of numbers, it's five anchors spaced about two orders of magnitude apart: L1 cache at a nanosecond, main memory at a hundred, SSD at a hundred microseconds, a same-datacenter round trip at half a millisecond, and a cross-continent round trip at a hundred and fifty milliseconds. Once those are internalised you stop debating whether to cache and start calculating it — a network call is roughly five thousand memory reads, so anything in a hot loop that crosses the network is a design error you can spot without profiling.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why memorise orders of magnitude rather than precise figures?

Because the precise figures go stale and the ratios don't. NVMe latency has improved by more than an order of magnitude in a decade, and cloud inter-AZ latency varies by provider and region — quoting a specific microsecond figure from memory invites a challenge you'll lose. The gaps are stable properties of physics: memory stays roughly a hundred times slower than L1 because of how far the signal travels on silicon, and a cross-continent round trip stays roughly a hundred thousand times slower than memory because of the speed of light in glass.

Design decisions are driven almost entirely by the gaps. Whether an SSD read is 16 or 100 microseconds rarely changes an architecture; whether it's microseconds or milliseconds absolutely does, because that's the difference between "serve it from disk" and "you need a cache". So the working knowledge is the shape of the ladder, and precise numbers are something you measure when a specific decision turns on them.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Where would you put a cache, and when would you decide not to?

I'd place it at the largest gap the request path crosses, because that's where a cache buys the most per unit of complexity. If the path does a same-DC database query for data that changes hourly, the gap between a ~500 µs network round trip and a ~100 ns in-process lookup is about 5,000×, and an in-process cache is both the cheapest and the most effective option. If the data must be shared across instances, a Redis hop is still same-DC — so you've traded a 5,000× win for maybe a 2× win over the database, which is often still worth it for load-shedding but is a completely different value proposition, and worth saying out loud rather than assuming.

I'd decide against caching when invalidation cost exceeds the latency win. If the data changes more often than it's read, a cache is pure overhead plus a correctness risk. If a stale read causes user-visible incorrectness — a balance, a permission check, an inventory count — the cache has converted a latency problem into a correctness problem, a bad trade at almost any speedup. Caching buys latency with staleness; the question is always whether this data can afford to be wrong for the TTL.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Operation Order of magnitude Scaled: if L1 = 1 second
L1 cache reference ~1 ns 1 second
Main memory (RAM) reference ~100 ns ~1.5 minutes
NVMe SSD random read ~100 µs ~1 day
Round trip, same datacenter ~500 µs ~6 days
Round trip, cross-region (same continent) ~50 ms ~1.6 years
Round trip, cross-continent ~150 ms ~5 years

⚠️ Orders of magnitude for reasoning, not benchmarks. The right-hand column is exact arithmetic on the left-hand column — its job is to make the gaps feel as large as they are, because the raw units flatten them.

6. Algorithm & Math (How the Mechanism Works)

No algorithm — the mechanism is a scale, and the point is the spacing between rungs.

The ladder, with the gap between each rung made explicit:

   1 ns  │█                                  L1 cache
 100 ns  │███                        ×100    RAM
 100 µs  │██████████                 ×1000   NVMe SSD read
 500 µs  │████████████               ×5      Same-DC round trip
  50 ms  │████████████████████████   ×100    Cross-region round trip
 150 ms  │███████████████████████████×3      Cross-continent round trip
         └────────────────────────────────
          each block ≈ one order of magnitude

The two gaps that decide architectures:
  RAM → same-DC network   ≈ 5,000×    → this is why you cache
  same-DC → cross-continent ≈ 300×    → this is why you replicate

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

Don't quote these as measurements. They're planning anchors. A senior engineer says "a network hop is three or four orders of magnitude above a memory read, so this loop can't do one" — not "a network hop is 500 microseconds", which invites a correction about your specific environment.

Don't use them to justify micro-optimisation. The ladder tells you where the large wins are, and they are almost never in the nanosecond rungs. Optimising memory access patterns while the request path makes six sequential cross-region calls is optimising the wrong end.

Don't assume the network numbers hold under load. All of these are quiet-system figures. Queuing delay grows non-linearly with utilisation, so a 500 µs same-DC RTT can become milliseconds at peak, which is exactly when it matters. The tail is a different number from the median and this table only gives you the median.

Don't forget the numbers below the network rungs move. Storage in particular has improved dramatically and continues to; a table memorised years ago will have the SSD rung badly wrong in absolute terms even though its position relative to RAM and network is roughly intact.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Redis is fast, so a Redis call is cheap."

✅ Reality: Redis is fast at the server, typically tens of microseconds of work. The call is a network round trip, so from the caller's perspective it costs a same-DC RTT — roughly 5,000× a local memory read, and the server's own speed is a small fraction of what you pay. This is why an in-process cache in front of Redis is often worth it, and why N sequential Redis calls in a loop is a latency bug regardless of how fast Redis is.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning):

❌ I grouped "disk" and "network" together as the two slow things, and treated them as roughly comparable.

✅ An NVMe read (~100 µs) and a same-DC round trip (~500 µs) are within an order of magnitude of each other, but a cross-continent round trip (~150 ms) is a thousand times worse than either. The meaningful split isn't disk-versus-network, it's local-versus-remote-versus-distant — and once I saw it that way, "read from local disk" stopped feeling like a fallback and started being a legitimately fast option.
